710189.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-? Proto-Indo-European *-tḗr Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr Proto-Hellenic *patḗr Ancient Greek πατήρ From Proto-Hellenic *patḗr (compare Mycenaean Greek 𐀞𐀳 (pa-te)), from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr.

710148.t: Conventionally derived from Proto-Hellenic *parsteno-, from Proto-Indo-European *pr̥-stén-o-s (with development of PIE *-rst- > Greek -ρθ- (-rth-)), from *pstḗn (“breast”).

710122.t: Borrowed from a foreign eastern language. Compare various Indo-Iranian terms like Sogdian 𐼾𐼴𐽀𐼹𐼻𐼸 (pwrδnk), Bactrian πορλαγγο-ζινο (porlango-zino), Pashto پړانګ (pṛāng), Persian پلنگ (palang), and Sanskrit पृदाकु (pṛ́dāku).

710187.t: Related to πάτος (pátos, “path”); see there for more.

710103.t: From παρα- (para-) + σκευάζω (skeuázō, “to make, prepare”) or παρασκευή (paraskeuḗ) + -άζω (-ázō).

710177.t: First attested in Mycenean Greek as 𐀞𐀯 (pa-si, equivalent to πᾶσι (pâsĭ)).

710182.t: Borrowed from Aramaic פַּסְחָא (pasḥā), from Biblical Hebrew פֶּסַח (pésaḥ).

710160.t: From πάροιμος (pároimos, “by the road, neighbor”) + -ία (-ía), or from παρα- (para-, “next, near, alongside, nearby, nigh”) + οἴμη (oímē, “song, tale”) + -ία (-ía, feminine suffix of abstraction).

710165.t: From παροξύνω (paroxúnō, “to sharpen, irritate”) + -μός (-mós), from παρά (pará, “beside”) + ὀξύνω (oxúnō, “to sharpen”).

710183.t: The four principal parts of the verb display the e-grade, o-grade, and zero-grade (πενθ-, πονθ-, παθ- (penth-, ponth-, path-)) of a root of uncertain identity.

710185.t: Possibly, from the same Pre-Greek root of πάταγος (pátagos, “clatter, crash”).

710107.t: From παρατάσσω (paratássō, “to place side by side”) + -σις (-sis).

710141.t: From παρα- (pără-, “by, near”) + ἔρχομαι (érkhomai, “to come, go”).

710119.t: Univerbation of παρά (părắ) and χρῆμα (khrêmă, “matter, affair”).

710178.t: This word is usually derived from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ- (“to attach”) (given by Beekes as *ph₂k- (“stiff, hard”)).

710109.t: From παρα- (para-, “beside, by”) + τείνω (teínō, “to stretch out”).
